words: Ná gonat ind fir in boin

words.lemma: gonaid (3pl. pres. subj./ipv., 'let them not wound/kill')

cognate: OIr. gonaid 'wounds, kills' = Ved. han- (*gʷʰen-); OIr. bó, acc. boin = Ved. gā́m (*gʷṓm); compound OIr. Bó-guine 'cow-slayer/-slaying' ~ Ved. go-hán-, go-ghná- ~ Gk βου-φόνος, βουφονέω
drift_or_renewal: none in Irish and Vedic; Greek keeps the collocation only in the compound (βουφονέω 'slaughter oxen', sacrificial/feast sense, not offence)
shared_syntax: verb *gʷʰen- with the cow (acc. *gʷōm) as direct object; also nominal compound *gʷou-gʷʰon- / -gʷʰn-o- (Ved. gohán-/goghná-, OIr. bóguine, Gk βουφόνος)
context: In both Irish and Vedic the killing of a (particular) cow is framed as a grave wrong that a speaker forbids or curses: Irish 'let the men not kill the cow' (the cow being a druid in cow-shape, Expulsion of the Déisi), and guin bó m-blicht 'slaying milch cows' in a Dindshenchas list of misdeeds; AV 1.16.4 curses whoever 'kills our cow, our horse, our man', and RV 1.114.10 / 7.56.17 pray that the god's 'cow-killing, man-killing' weapon stay far off. Exact cognates for both members plus the matching compound in three branches make chance unlikely, though 'kill a cow' is semantically simple, so the inherited element is the fixed collocation/compound rather than a poetic figure.

words: diruawryon lafuryeu ar vor a thir

support.locus: Wordsworth, Fragments and Specimens of Early Latin, annalistic fragment

cognate: OIr. muir = Lat. mare, MW môr (*mori-); OIr. tír, MW tir = Lat. terra (*ters- 'dry (land)')
drift_or_renewal: Greek renews both members (κατὰ γῆν καὶ κατὰ θάλασσαν, e.g. Thuc. 4.118.5 in bundle BS-c36db); Irish has a variant with talam for tír
shared_syntax: coordinated merism 'sea and land' (Lat. terra marique, per maria ac terras; OIr. for muir ⁊ (for) tír, eter muir ⁊ tír; MW ar vor a thir) as an adverbial of totality, esp. of toil/suffering or campaigning 'by sea and land'
context: The Immram Brain pivot sets sea against land (do-snig a mmuir fri tír toinn) in a description of the world; Lucretius uses the merism for the whole world under Venus. The OIr. saga verse 'what I suffered of trouble on sea and land' (Siaburcharpat) and MW 'great toils on sea and land' match Latin 'terra marique' of deeds/toils. The match is in both members cognate, which narrows it to Italic and Celtic (tír/terra is an Italo-Celtic lexical isogloss); but the merism is natural, and Irish and Welsh clerical writers knew Latin 'terra marique', so borrowing of the phrase cannot be excluded.

cognate: OIr. nigid = Ved. nij- = Gk νίζω (*neigʷ-); OIr. ech = Ved. áśva- (*h₁eḱwos); OIr. uisce ~ Gk ὕδωρ (*wed-/ud-)
drift_or_renewal: Vedic renews 'water' as nadī́ṣu 'in the rivers'; Greek keeps verb + water (νίζ' ὕδατι) but not with the horse (Homer washes horses with λούω)
shared_syntax: passive of *neigʷ- with the horse as subject, with the water as instrument/source
context: LU battle poem on Diarmait: blood has fallen into 'the water in which Grip, i.e. Diarmait's horse, is washed', so it is no longer pure for the sacrament; RV has the recurrent simile 'like a horse washed (in the rivers)' for Soma being purified. Both are purity contexts, but horse-washing is everyday practice and the Irish is a gloss, so the match may be chance.

note: All 247 bundles read in order. Most hold only shared generic roots. Leads checked and dropped: snigid gaim ~ ORu зима/снѣгъ (generic weather), coin fri míla maige ~ κύνες περὶ μῆλα (dog + *smeh1lo-, contexts differ), eoch liath ~ fölvan jó, blegon na mbó ~ mjólka kýr, kin triad father-mother-brothers (Ingcél ~ RV 10.34.4), fuine ar beraib ~ Umbr. berva (lexical only).
